items.title: A phase domain, its canonical one-form and its standard symplectic two-form
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.1 (Hamilton's equations and canonical coordinates: lambda = sum p_i dq^i, omega = sum dq^i wedge dp_i), printed pages 80-88

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Sections 15.1-15.2 (Hamiltonian mechanics in phase space and the symplectic structure)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$. A **phase domain** is a nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Its points are written $z=(q,p)$ with
$q=(q^1,\dots,q^n)\in\mathbb R^n$ and $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in\mathbb R^n$; the coordinate functions
$q^i,p_i:U\to\mathbb R$ are smooth ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
$\partial_{q^1},\dots,\partial_{q^n},\partial_{p_1},\dots,\partial_{p_n}$ is the coordinate frame
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). On a phase domain:

1. the **canonical one-form** is the smooth one-form
   $\lambda_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,dq^i\in\Omega^1(U)$;
2. the **standard symplectic two-form** is the smooth two-form
   $\omega_U:=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i\in\Omega^2(U)$
   ([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]);
3. the **standard symplectic matrix** is the block matrix
   $$J:=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R),$$
   whose blocks are $n\times n$.

The identity $\omega_U=-d\lambda_U$ holds, because the coordinate formula for the exterior
derivative ([[thm-local-coordinate-formula-for-the-exterior-derivative]]) gives
$d\lambda_U=\sum_i dp_i\wedge dq^i=-\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$. When $U$ is an induced chart domain of a
cotangent bundle, the published [[def-tautological-one-form-on-a-cotangent-bundle]] identifies
$\lambda_U$ and $\omega_U$ with the tautological one-form and the canonical cotangent two-form in
those coordinates; the present definition is the choice-free local coordinate model that the
canonical-calculus items of this page use.

items.title: Finite-regularity differential forms, Hamiltonian fields and canonical maps in phase charts
items.design_state: owner-accepted local definition

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics, Sections 4.1 and 4.4: coordinate Hamiltonian fields and the symplectic Jacobian condition

items.statement:
Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ be phase domains with standard forms and matrix $J$ of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]. All finite differentiability classes and diffeomorphisms use [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

On any open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a **$C^k$ coordinate differential form**, $k\ge0$, is a sum $\sum_{i_1<\cdots<i_j}a_{i_1\cdots i_j}(z)\,dz^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dz^{i_j}$ with $C^k$ coefficient functions. Its value at a point is the indicated alternating multilinear form on $\mathbb R^m$. For $k\ge1$ define its exterior derivative by the coordinate formula $d(a\,dz^{i_1}\wedge\cdots)=\sum_l(\partial_l a)\,dz^l\wedge dz^{i_1}\wedge\cdots$, extended linearly. For a $C^1$ map $C:U\to V$, the **pointwise pullback** is
$$ (C^*\eta)_z(v_1,\ldots,v_j):=\eta_{C(z)}(DC(z)v_1,\ldots,DC(z)v_j). $$
It is a continuous form when $\eta$ is continuous; no assertion that this pullback is smooth is part of the definition. Wedges and contractions are the pointwise alternating multilinear operations. Thus the finite-regularity identities below can be read without applying a definition restricted to smooth forms or maps.

A **$C^r$ canonical map**, $1\le r\le\infty$, is a $C^r$ map $C:U\to V$ satisfying $C^*\omega_V=\omega_U$ pointwise. A **$C^r$ canonical transformation** is such a map that is a $C^r$ diffeomorphism onto $V$; a **local $C^r$ canonical transformation** is a $C^r$ local diffeomorphism satisfying the same equality. The $C^\infty$ case agrees with [[def-canonical-transformation]] and [[def-symplectomorphism-local-symplectomorphism-and-symplectic-embedding]]; the finite-$r$ terminology on this page is the definition just given, and does not assert that a $C^1$ map is smooth.

For $h\in C^2(U)$ the **coordinate Hamiltonian field** is the $C^1$ vector-valued map $X_h:=J\nabla h$, viewed as a field by the canonical identification $T_zU=\mathbb R^{2n}$. Its characterization by $\iota_{X_h}\omega_U=dh$ is proved in [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]. For $f,g\in C^1(U)$ define the **coordinate Poisson bracket** by $\{f,g\}:=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\nabla g$; for $C^2$ inputs it is $C^1$ and equals $\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ by that proposition. Smooth inputs recover the smooth symplectic conventions. No closure of the $C^2$ class under this bracket is assumed.

items.title: The standard two-form of a phase domain is closed and nondegenerate, with contraction $\iota_v\omega=\sum_i a_i\,dp_i-\sum_i b_i\,dq^i$
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: Ana Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, revised January 2006, Symplectic Manifolds (the symplectic form sum dq^i wedge dp_i on R^2n, closedness and nondegeneracy) and Lecture 18

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.1 (Hamilton's equations: contraction identities and the matrix epsilon used for the symplectic form), printed pages 80-88

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with canonical one-form $\lambda_U$, standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ and matrix $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_n&I_n\\-I_n&0_n\end{pmatrix}$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]). For a point $z\in U$ write
$\omega_z:=(\omega_U)_z$. Then:

1. $\omega_U$ is closed: $d\omega_U=0$;
2. for all $v,w\in\mathbb R^{2n}$, written in the coordinate frame as $v=(a,b)$ and $w=(c,d)$ with
   $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb R^n$, one has
   $$\omega_z(v,w)=v^{\mathsf T}J\,w=a\cdot d-b\cdot c ;$$
3. for every $v=(a,b)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ the contraction is the covector
   $$\iota_v\omega_z=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dp_i-\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\,dq^i ;$$
4. $J^{\mathsf T}=-J$, $J^2=-I_{2n}$, and $J$ is invertible with $J^{-1}=J^{\mathsf T}=-J$;
5. consequently $v\mapsto\iota_v\omega_z$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathbb R^{2n}\to(\mathbb R^{2n})^*$,
   so $\omega_U$ is nondegenerate at every point and $(U,\omega_U)$ is a symplectic manifold.

items.title: The Hamiltonian field of a $C^2$ function on a phase domain is $J\nabla H$, and the Poisson bracket is $\sum_i(\partial_{q^i}f\,\partial_{p_i}g-\partial_{p_i}f\,\partial_{q^i}g)$
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Sections 4.1 (Hamilton's equations from iota_X omega = dH) and 4.3 (Poisson brackets and the coordinate formula), printed pages 80-99

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.3 (canonical transformations and the Hamiltonian field in phase-space coordinates)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form
$\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), and let
$H:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Write
$\nabla H=(H_{q^1},\dots,H_{q^n},H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n})$ for the Euclidean gradient
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $J$ for the standard symplectic matrix. Then:

1. there is exactly one $C^1$ vector field $X_H$ on $U$ with $\iota_{X_H}\omega_U=dH$, and it is
   $$X_H=J\nabla H=\bigl(H_{p_1},\dots,H_{p_n},-H_{q^1},\dots,-H_{q^n}\bigr);$$
2. an integral curve $t\mapsto(q(t),p(t))$ of $X_H$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $$\dot q^i=H_{p_i}(q,p),\qquad \dot p_i=-H_{q^i}(q,p)\qquad(i=1,\dots,n);$$
3. for $f,g\in C^2(U)$ the Poisson bracket
   $\{f,g\}:=\omega_U(X_f,X_g)$ (in the finite-regularity convention of [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]) is
   $$\{f,g\}=\nabla f^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(f_{q^i}g_{p_i}-f_{p_i}g_{q^i}\bigr),$$
   hence $\{f,g\}=-\{g,f\}$, and $\{f,g\}$ is $C^1$ on $U$.

items.title: The derivative of the Hamiltonian flow satisfies $Y^{\mathsf T}JY=J$ and $\det Y=1$
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Sections 4.1-4.2 (the linearised flow of Hamilton's equations and Liouville's theorem), printed pages 80-92

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Sections 15.1-15.2 (the canonical equations and the divergence-free Hamiltonian flow)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U$ be a phase domain with standard two-form $\omega_U$ and matrix $J$, let
$H\in C^2(U)$, and let $\Phi$ be the local flow of the Hamiltonian field
$X_H=J\nabla H$ ([[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]],
[[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]). Let $z_0\in U$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be the open
interval of times $t$ with $(t,z_0)$ in the flow domain, and for $t\in I$ put

$$Y(t):=D_z\Phi_t(z_0)\in M_{2n}(\mathbb R).$$

Then $t\mapsto Y(t)$ is of class $C^1$ on $I$ and, for every $t\in I$:

1. (variational equation) $Y'(t)=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H(\Phi_t(z_0))\,Y(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_{2n}$;
2. (canonical matrix identity) $Y(t)^{\mathsf T}J\,Y(t)=J$;
3. (unit determinant) $\det Y(t)=1$.

The same conclusions hold for a **time-dependent Hamiltonian** $\mathcal H:T\times U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, where $T$ is an open real interval. For $t_0\in T$ and $z_0\in U$, write $E(t,t_0,z)$ for the maximal solution of $z'=J\nabla_z\mathcal H(t,z)$ with $z(t_0)=z$; its domain consists of the triples where this solution exists. On the maximal open time interval $I_{t_0,z_0}$ set $Y(t)=D_zE(t,t_0,z_0)$. Then
$$Y'=J\,\operatorname{Hess}_z\mathcal H(t,E(t,t_0,z_0))Y,\qquad Y(t_0)=I_{2n},\qquad Y^{\mathsf T}JY=J,\qquad\det Y=1.$$
The evolution $E$ is $C^1$ on its open domain, and each fixed-endpoint map has inverse $E(t_0,t,\cdot)$ on its image. Autonomous $H$ is recovered by $\mathcal H(t,z)=H(z)$ and $E(t,t_0,z)=\Phi(t-t_0,z)$.

items.title: A Hamiltonian local flow on a phase domain preserves Lebesgue measure on its flow domain
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.2 (Liouville's theorem: the flow of Hamilton's equations preserves phase-space volume), printed pages 88-92
Ana Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, revised January 2006, canonical symplectomorphisms preserve the symplectic volume form omega^n / n!

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice where the cited change-of-variables theorem requires it
([[def-countable-choice]], [[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]). Let $n\ge1$, let
$U$ be a phase domain ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]), let
$H\in C^2(U)$, and let $\Phi$ be the local flow of $X_H=J\nabla H$
([[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]). Let $t\in\mathbb R$, let
$D_t:=\{z\in U:(t,z)\text{ lies in the flow domain}\}$ be the open domain of $\Phi_t$
([[cor-cm-flow-domain-open-and-flow-is-c1]]), and let $A\subseteq D_t$ be a bounded Borel set with
$\overline A\subseteq D_t$. Then $A$ and $\Phi_t(A)$ are Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_{2n}\bigl(\Phi_t(A)\bigr)=\lambda_{2n}(A).$$

For a $C^2$ time-dependent Hamiltonian $\mathcal H:T\times U\to\mathbb R$ and the evolution $E$ of [[prop-cm-flow-derivative-satisfies-the-canonical-matrix-identity]], fix $t_0,t\in T$. Its initial-state domain $D_{t,t_0}=\{z:E(t,t_0,z)\text{ is defined}\}$ is open. For every bounded Borel $A\subseteq D_{t,t_0}$ with $\overline A\subseteq D_{t,t_0}$,
$$\lambda_{2n}(E(t,t_0,A))=\lambda_{2n}(A).$$
No completeness or time independence is needed.

items.title: Generating functions of the first and second kind for a local canonical map
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.4.3 'Generating Functions' (the four kinds of generating function and the relations p = dS_1/dq, P = -dS_1/dQ), printed pages 104-105

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.3 (canonical transformations in Hamiltonian mechanics and their generating functions)

items.statement:
**First-kind data.** Let $n\ge1$ and let $O_q,O_Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets
([[def-metric-topology]]). Let $S:O_q\times O_Q\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and assume

$$\det S_{qQ}(q,Q)\ne0\qquad\bigl((q,Q)\in O_q\times O_Q\bigr),$$

where $S_{qQ}(q,Q)$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries
$\partial^2 S/\partial q^i\partial Q^j(q,Q)$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). Identify $O_q\times O_Q$ with the phase-domain coordinates
$(q,Q)$ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]) and form the
$C^2$ map

$$\Psi:O_q\times O_Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{2n},\qquad \Psi(q,Q):=\bigl(q,\ S_q(q,Q)\bigr),$$

whose derivative is the block matrix
$D\Psi(q,Q)=\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}(q,Q)&S_{qQ}(q,Q)\end{pmatrix}$. A **generating function of
the first kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is, on a neighbourhood of a point
$(q_*,Q_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,Q),\qquad P:=-S_Q(q,Q),$$

solved as follows: since $\det S_{qQ}\ne0$, the inverse function theorem
([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]) makes $\Psi$ a local $C^2$ diffeomorphism, so
$p=S_q(q,Q)$ determines a $C^2$ local inverse $Q=Q(q,p)$ on a neighbourhood of
$\Psi(q_*,Q_*)$; then $C(q,p):=(Q(q,p),-S_Q(q,Q(q,p)))$.

**Second-kind data.** Let $O_q,O_P\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets and let
$S:O_q\times O_P\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$ with $\det S_{qP}(q,P)\ne0$ everywhere. A
**generating function of the second kind** is such an $S$; the **local map generated by $S$** is,
near a point $(q_*,P_*)$, the $C^2$ map $C:(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ defined by

$$p:=S_q(q,P),\qquad Q:=S_P(q,P),$$

where again the relation $p=S_q(q,P)$ is solved locally for $P=P(q,p)$ by the inverse function
theorem applied to $(q,P)\mapsto(q,S_q(q,P))$, whose derivative is
$\begin{pmatrix}I_n&0\\ S_{qq}&S_{qP}\end{pmatrix}$.

**Recorded identities.** Wherever $S$ is of the first kind, the identity
$p\,dq-P\,dQ=dS$ holds; wherever $S$ is of the second kind, the identity $p\,dq+Q\,dP=dS$ holds,
both as identities of $C^2$ coordinate one-forms on the $(q,Q)$- resp. $(q,P)$-space with $p,P,Q$ read as the
displayed functions ([[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]]). The mixed-derivative hypotheses
$\det S_{qQ}\ne0$ resp. $\det S_{qP}\ne0$ are part of the data.

items.title: The local map generated by a first- or second-kind generating function is a canonical $C^2$ local diffeomorphism
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.3 (canonical transformations generated by a function of the old and new coordinates)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ and let $S$ be a generating function of the first kind or of the second kind, with data
$O_q,O_Q$ resp. $O_q,O_P$ and the local map $C$ it generates
([[def-cm-generating-function-of-the-first-and-second-kind]]). Then $C$ is a $C^2$ local
diffeomorphism and it is canonical: on its domain,

$$C^*\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n dQ^i\wedge dP_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i=1}^n dq^i\wedge dp_i .$$

Moreover $|\det DC|=1$ wherever $C$ is defined
([[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]).

The words canonical and the finite-regularity form operations here use [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]], with the displayed $C^2$ maps; smoothness is not inferred.

items.title: A canonical map with invertible $(q,Q)$-projection is locally generated by a first-kind generating function
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.4.3 'Generating Functions' (existence of a generating function on a neighbourhood where the relevant projection is a diffeomorphism), printed pages 104-105

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.3 (canonical transformations and the local existence of a generating function)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ be phase domains with standard two-forms
$\omega_U,\omega_V$, and let $C:U\to V$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism with $C^*\omega_V=\omega_U$
([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]],
[[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]). Write $C(z)=(Q(z),P(z))$ and
$z=(q(z),p(z))$ for the coordinate functions, and let $z_0\in U$. If the map
$$F:U\to\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n,\qquad F(z):=\bigl(q(z),Q(z)\bigr)$$
has invertible derivative at $z_0$, then there are an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq U$ of $z_0$ and
an open ball $W''\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ about $F(z_0)$ with $F(W)=W''$ on which
$F$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, and a $C^3$ function $S:W''\to\mathbb R$ with
$\det S_{qQ}(F(z_0))\ne0$, such that the restriction of $S$ to a product neighbourhood $O_q\times O_Q\subseteq W''$ of $F(z_0)$ is a first-kind generating function and its generated local map agrees with $C$ on a neighbourhood of $z_0$.

The words canonical and the finite-regularity form operations here use [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]], with the displayed $C^2$ maps; smoothness is not inferred.

items.title: A time-dependent generating function produces canonical time slices and shifts the Hamiltonian by $S_t$
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.4.3 'Generating Functions' (time-dependent generating functions and the Hamiltonian shift K = H + dS/dt), printed pages 104-105

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.3 (time-dependent canonical transformations generated by a function of the old and new coordinates)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $O_q,O_Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
nonempty open sets ([[def-metric-topology]]), and let
$S:J\times O_q\times O_Q\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$ with
$\det S_{qQ}(t,q,Q)\ne0$ for every $(t,q,Q)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). For
each $t\in J$ let $S_t:=S(t,\cdot,\cdot)$ and let $C_t$ be the first-kind map generated by $S_t$
([[def-cm-generating-function-of-the-first-and-second-kind]]). Let
$H:J\times V\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ on a phase domain $V\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ such that $(q,S_q(t,q,Q))\in V$ for every $(t,q,Q)\in J\times O_q\times O_Q$; thus every Hamiltonian argument in the identity below is in its declared domain. Then:

1. for every $t\in J$ the map $C_t$ is a canonical $C^2$ local diffeomorphism
   ([[prop-cm-generating-functions-yield-canonical-maps]]);
2. on $J\times O_q\times O_Q$, with $p:=S_q(t,q,Q)$, $P:=-S_Q(t,q,Q)$ and
   $K(t,q,Q):=H\bigl(t,q,S_q(t,q,Q)\bigr)+S_t(t,q,Q)$, the one-form identity
   $$p\,dq-H(t,q,p)\,dt=P\,dQ-K\,dt+dS$$
   holds identically: on the region where both descriptions are defined, the Poincare-Cartan
   one-forms of $H$ and of $K=H+S_t$ differ by the exact form $dS$, with all quantities read as
   functions of $(t,q,Q)$.

The words canonical and the finite-regularity form operations here use [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]], with the displayed $C^2$ maps; smoothness is not inferred.

items.title: The symplectic shift of the cylinder changes $\lambda$ by the closed, non-exact form $a\,d\theta$ and has no global generating function
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Sections 4.4.3 (generating functions) and 4.5 (action-angle variables: the cylinder as the phase space of an angle variable with a shift symmetry), printed pages 104-112
Ana Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, revised January 2006, Lecture 18 (integrable systems and the affine structure of the flow on tori)

items.statement:
Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with quotient map
$q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]), let
$C:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb R$ be the cylinder, and identify $C$ with the quotient of $\mathbb R^2$
by the deck transformation $\tau(\theta,I)=(\theta+1,I)$, with quotient map
$\pi:\mathbb R^2\to C$ ([[def-quotient-topology]]); assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ where the cited
torus definition requires it. Give $\mathbb T$ the smooth structure generated by the lift charts $(q(J), (q|_J)^{-1})$ for open intervals $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ of length less than one, and give $C$ their product charts with the real coordinate $I$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). The quotient map is open because $q^{-1}(q(V))=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(V+k)$ for open $V$; thus $q|_J$ is a homeomorphism onto an open set. Chart transitions are locally translations by integers and leave $I$ unchanged, hence are smooth. Hausdorffness and a countable base follow from the torus supplier and the real coordinate, so these charts specify a smooth cylinder and $\pi$ is a surjective local diffeomorphism. Since $d\theta\wedge dI$ and $I\,d\theta$ are invariant under $\tau$,
the expressions in each lift chart agree on overlaps (integer translations fix their differentials and $I$), and hence define unique smooth forms $\omega_C,\lambda_C$ on $C$ with
$\pi^*\omega_C=d\theta\wedge dI$ and $\pi^*\lambda_C=I\,d\theta$; while $d\theta$ descends to a
smooth one-form $d\theta_C$ on $C$ with $\pi^*d\theta_C=d\theta$. Let $a\ne0$ and let
$\Phi:C\to C$ be the **symplectic shift** given in quotient coordinates by
$\Phi(\theta,I)=(\theta,I+a)$. Then:

1. $\Phi$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism, $\Phi^*\omega_C=\omega_C$, and
   $\Phi^*\lambda_C=\lambda_C+a\,d\theta_C$;
2. $a\,d\theta_C$ is closed but not exact: there is no $C^1$ function $W:C\to\mathbb R$ with
   $dW=a\,d\theta_C$;
3. for every point of $C$ there is a neighbourhood on which $\Phi$ is generated by the second-kind
   generating function $S(\theta,P)=\theta P-a\theta$, but there is no $C^1$ function
   $S:(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ whose generated map is $\Phi$; the local
   generating functions do not glue to a global one.

items.title: The Hamilton-Jacobi equation and a complete integral of it
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.7 'The Hamilton-Jacobi Equation' (the equation W_t + H(q, W_q, t) = 0 and the role of dW/dbeta constants), printed pages 121-126

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.4 (Hamilton-Jacobi theory and Jacobi's complete integral)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval
([[def-interval]]), let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty open set, and let

$$H:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); write $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ for
the third variable, so that $(t,q,p)$ range over phase-type data and $H$ is a Hamiltonian in the
sense of [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]. Let
$J'\subseteq J$, $U'\subseteq U$ and $A'\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets
([[def-metric-topology]]) and let $S:J'\times U'\times A'\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^3$; write
$\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)$ for the third variable.

$S$ **solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$** on $J'\times U'\times A'$ if

$$S_t(t,q,\alpha)+H\bigl(t,\,q,\,S_q(t,q,\alpha)\bigr)=0\qquad\bigl((t,q,\alpha)\in J'\times U'\times A'\bigr),$$

where $S_t$ is the partial derivative in $t$, $S_q=(S_{q^1},\dots,S_{q^n})$ is the gradient in $q$
and $H$ is evaluated at the momentum $p=S_q(t,q,\alpha)$
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]). $S$ is a
**complete integral** of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation at $(t_0,q_0,\alpha_0)$ if in addition

$$\det S_{q\alpha}(t_0,q_0,\alpha_0)\ne0,$$

where $S_{q\alpha}$ is the $n\times n$ matrix with entries
$\partial^2S/\partial q^i\partial\alpha_j$, called the **mixed derivative**.

If $S$ is a complete integral, the associated **momentum map** is
$p(t,q,\alpha):=S_q(t,q,\alpha)$ and the associated **constants**
$\beta(t,q,\alpha):=S_\alpha(t,q,\alpha)$ are the **Jacobi constants** of the complete integral.
This is the Hamiltonian case of the general first-order equation $u_t+H(t,q,D_qu)=0$: the $n$
parameters $\alpha$ enter essentially through the nonvanishing mixed derivative, and $S_t$ is
determined algebraically by $S_q$ on the solutions.

items.title: A complete integral produces Hamilton characteristics, the Jacobi constants, a local converse and canonical $(\beta,\alpha)$ labels
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.7 (from a solution W of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, the equations q-dot = H_p with p = W_q reproduce Hamilton's second equation; the constants dW/dbeta), printed pages 121-126

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.4 (Hamilton-Jacobi theory: Jacobi's complete integral and its constants)

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and
$A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty open sets, let $H:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be of
class $C^2$, and let $S:J\times U\times A\to\mathbb R$ be a $C^3$ complete integral of the
Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with $H$ at $(t_0,q_0,\alpha_0)\in J\times U\times A$
([[def-cm-hamilton-jacobi-equation-and-complete-integral]]); write $\beta_0:=S_\alpha(t_0,q_0,\alpha_0)$.
Then:

1. (characteristics) for every $\alpha$ sufficiently close to $\alpha_0$ there is an open interval
   $I_\alpha\ni t_0$ and a curve $q:I_\alpha\to U$ with $q(t_0)=q_0$ solving
   $q'(t)=H_p\bigl(t,q(t),S_q(t,q(t),\alpha)\bigr)$, and with $p(t):=S_q(t,q(t),\alpha)$ the pair
   $(q,p)$ solves Hamilton's equations $q'=H_p$, $p'=-H_q$ on $I_\alpha$;
2. (Jacobi constants) $\beta(t):=S_\alpha(t,q(t),\alpha)$ is constant on $I_\alpha$, equal to
   $S_\alpha(t_0,q_0,\alpha)$;
3. (local converse) for $(\alpha,\beta)$ near $(\alpha_0,\beta_0)$ the equation
   $\beta=S_\alpha(t,q,\alpha)$ can be solved locally for $q=Q(t,\alpha,\beta)$, and with
   $p:=S_q(t,Q(t,\alpha,\beta),\alpha)$ the curve $t\mapsto(Q,p)$ solves Hamilton's equations;
4. (canonical labels) on the domain of the local diffeomorphism $(q,p)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$
   obtained by composing $(q,p)\mapsto(q,\alpha)$ with $(q,\alpha)\mapsto(\beta,\alpha)$, one has
   the two-form identity $dq\wedge dp=d\beta\wedge d\alpha$ at every fixed $t$; that is,
   $(\beta,\alpha)$ are local canonical coordinates, conjugate to $(q,p)$, in which the
   $\beta$ are constants of the motion of clause 2.

The words canonical and the finite-regularity form operations here use [[def-cm-finite-regularity-canonical-calculus]], with the displayed $C^2$ maps; smoothness is not inferred.

items.title: A closed smooth two-form on a star-shaped domain has the radial primitive $\alpha_x(v)=\int_0^1 t\,\tau_{tx}(x,v)\,dt$
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: John M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, second edition, Theorem 17.14 and its proof (the homotopy formula gives the radial primitive of a closed form on a star-shaped domain)
Nigel Hitchin, Differentiable Manifolds (2014), the Poincare lemma and the explicit radial contraction formula

items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be an open set star-shaped with respect to $0$
([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), and let $\tau$ be a smooth closed two-form on $U$
([[def-smooth-differential-k-form]], [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]]). Write
$\tau=\sum_{i<j}\tau_{ij}\,dx^i\wedge dx^j$ with smooth coefficient functions $\tau_{ij}$, and extend
the coefficients by $\tau_{ji}:=-\tau_{ij}$ and $\tau_{ii}:=0$. Define
$\alpha:U\to(\mathbb R^n)^*$ by

$$\alpha_x(v):=\int_0^1 t\,\tau_{tx}(x,v)\,dt .$$

Then $\alpha$ is a smooth one-form on $U$, in coordinates

$$\alpha=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,dx^i,\qquad \alpha_i(x)=\int_0^1 t\sum_{j=1}^n x^j\,\tau_{ji}(tx)\,dt ,$$

and $d\alpha=\tau$ on $U$. In particular every smooth closed two-form on a star-shaped
open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ is exact, with the displayed explicit primitive.

items.title: Action-angle coordinates on a saturated proper submersion neighbourhood of a compact connected regular fibre, with the two-form primitive supplied locally
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: Ana Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, revised January 2006, Lecture 18, Definition 18.10, Lemma 18.11 and Theorem 18.12 (Arnold-Liouville), pp. 110-111
Eckhard Meinrenken, Symplectic Geometry, Chapter 6, sections 6.1-6.3, Theorem 6.21 (action-angle coordinates), pp. 66-75

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.5 'Action-Angle Variables' (integrable systems and the construction of action-angle variables), printed pages 105-112

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(M,\omega)$
be a symplectic manifold of dimension $2n$, let $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n)$ be a completely integrable
system on $M$ ([[def-completely-integrable-hamiltonian-system]]) and let $N=F^{-1}(b_0)$ be a
nonempty compact connected regular fibre. Assume that, after restricting to a saturated
neighbourhood $U$ of $N$ and a ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of regular values with $F(U)=B$, the map
$\pi:=F|_U:U\to B$ is a proper submersion with connected fibres. Then there are an open neighbourhood $B_0\subseteq B$ of $b_0$, an open action-coordinate ball $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and, on the shrunk saturated neighbourhood $U_0:=\pi^{-1}(B_0)$, action-angle coordinates
$(I,\theta):U_0\to A\times T^n$ in the sense of [[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]] (period-one
angles) with

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i\wedge dI_i ,$$

and every $C^\infty$ function on $U_0$ that is constant on the fibres of $\pi$ (in particular each
$F_i|_{U_0}$) is a function of $I$ alone. The base neighbourhood $B_0$ is in the original integral-value coordinates, whereas $A=I(B_0)$ is in the action coordinates; they need not be the same set or both Euclidean balls.

Here $T^n=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ has the quotient topology and the smooth atlas generated by the inverses of the restrictions of $q_n:x\mapsto[x]$ to open boxes whose side lengths are less than one. The map $q_n$ is open, since the preimage of $q_n(V)$ is $\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}(V+k)$ for open $V$; its restriction to each such box is injective and a homeomorphism onto an open set. On each overlap component the chart transition is translation by a fixed integer vector, hence smooth. The quotient is Hausdorff and second countable as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]], so this atlas specifies a smooth manifold ([[def-smooth-manifold]]), and $q_n$ is a local diffeomorphism. The symbols $d\theta_i$ mean the global one-forms obtained from the differentials of these local lifts; integer translations leave those differentials unchanged. The product $A\times T^n$ carries the corresponding product charts.

items.title: Period-one to radian action-angle rescaling: $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}=2\pi\theta$ and $I^{\mathrm{rad}}=I/(2\pi)$ preserve $\omega$
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.5.3 (action-angle variables for one-dimensional systems and the 2 pi normalisation), printed pages 108-111
Ana Cannas da Silva, Lectures on Symplectic Geometry, revised January 2006, Lecture 18 (the Arnold-Liouville theorem; local period and sign conventions are specified here)

items.statement:
Let $(I,\theta)$ be period-one action-angle coordinates with
$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i\wedge dI_i$ as supplied by
[[thm-cm-liouville-arnold-action-angle-repaired]] and
[[def-action-and-angle-coordinates]]. Use the quotient lift charts and global angle differentials specified in [[thm-cm-liouville-arnold-action-angle-repaired]]. Put $T_{\mathrm{rad}}:=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$, with quotient lift charts from intervals of length less than $2\pi$; their transitions are translations by $2\pi k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$. The induced diffeomorphism $s:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is $s([x])=[2\pi x]$, with inverse $[y]\mapsto[y/(2\pi)]$. Thus the notation $2\pi\theta_i$ below means $s\circ\theta_i$, with values in $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$, and its differential is defined by local real lifts. The action domain rescales from $A$ to $A/(2\pi)$. Define the rescaled coordinates

$$\theta_i^{\mathrm{rad}}:=2\pi\,\theta_i,\qquad I_i^{\mathrm{rad}}:=\frac{I_i}{2\pi}\qquad(i=1,\dots,n).$$

Then $(\theta^{\mathrm{rad}},I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ are $C^\infty$ coordinates on the same chart,

$$\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\theta_i^{\mathrm{rad}}\wedge dI_i^{\mathrm{rad}},$$

the angles $\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}$ are $2\pi$-periodic (radian-valued), and if a Hamiltonian is
$H=h(I)$ with $h$ of class $C^2$ in the period-one coordinates then in the radian coordinates it is
$H=\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ with $\tilde h(I^{\mathrm{rad}})=h(2\pi I^{\mathrm{rad}})$ and
$\dot\theta^{\mathrm{rad}}_i=\partial\tilde h/\partial I^{\mathrm{rad}}_i$.

items.title: The free particle: the complete integral $S=q\alpha-t\alpha^2/(2m)$, its characteristics and its canonical labels
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 4.7 (the free particle as the simplest Hamilton-Jacobi example), printed pages 121-126

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Section 15.4 (Jacobi's complete integral and worked Hamilton-Jacobi examples)

items.statement:
Let $m>0$ and let $H:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$H(t,q,p):=p^2/(2m)$, be the free-particle Hamiltonian
([[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]]), and let
$S:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $S(t,q,\alpha):=q\alpha-t\alpha^2/(2m)$. Then:

1. $S$ solves the Hamilton-Jacobi equation $S_t+H(t,q,S_q)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and is a complete
   integral at every point, with $S_{q\alpha}=1$
   ([[def-cm-hamilton-jacobi-equation-and-complete-integral]]);
2. the Jacobi constants are $\beta:=S_\alpha=q-t\alpha/m$, so the characteristics are
   $q(t)=\beta+t\alpha/m$ with momentum $p=\alpha$; these satisfy $q'=p/m$, $p'=0$, and $\beta$ is
   constant along them ([[thm-cm-hamilton-jacobi-characteristics-from-a-complete-integral]]);
3. on $\mathbb R^3$ at fixed $t$ one has $dq\wedge dp=d\beta\wedge d\alpha$: the pair $(\beta,\alpha)$
   is canonically conjugate to $(q,p)$.

items.statement:
Let $n=1$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and let $S:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$,
$S(q,P):=qP+\lambda q^2/2$. Then:

1. $S$ is a generating function of the second kind with $S_{qP}=1\ne0$, and the local map it
   generates is $\Psi_\lambda(q,p)=(Q,P)=(q,\,p-\lambda q)$, defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$
   ([[def-cm-generating-function-of-the-first-and-second-kind]]);
2. $\Psi_\lambda$ is canonical, both by the generating-function theorem
   ([[prop-cm-generating-functions-yield-canonical-maps]]) and by direct verification of the matrix
   identity $D\Psi_\lambda^{\mathsf T}J\,D\Psi_\lambda=J$
   ([[prop-cm-canonical-map-tests-and-hamiltonian-transport]]).

items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Sections 15.3-15.4 (canonical transformations and their global behaviour)

items.statement:
Take the cylinder $C=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb R$ with the shift
$\Phi(\theta,I)=(\theta,I+1)$, i.e. $a=1$ in
[[prop-cm-cylinder-shift-has-no-global-generating-function]], and with the descended forms
$\lambda_C,\omega_C$ of that proposition. Then:

1. $\Phi^*\lambda_C=\lambda_C+d\theta_C$ and $\Phi^*\omega_C=\omega_C$;
2. the loop $\gamma(t)=\pi(t,0)$, $t\in[0,1]$, satisfies
   $\int_0^1 d\theta_C(\gamma'(t))\,dt=1\ne0$, confirming that $d\theta_C$ is not exact on $C$;
3. on the chart $\{\theta\in(0,1)\}$ the second-kind generating function
   $S(\theta,P)=\theta P-\theta$ generates the shift; globally no such $C^1$ function exists.

items.title: The isotropic oscillator: the explicit flow, $Y^{\mathsf T}JY=J$ and $\det Y=1$
items.design_state: completed local argument; carrier and readiness record authored in this batch

D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Sections 15.1-15.2 (phase-space flows of the harmonic oscillator)

items.statement:
Let $n=1$, $U=\mathbb R^2$ with coordinates $(q,p)$, and $H(q,p)=(p^2+q^2)/2$. Then:

1. $X_H=(p,-q)$ and its flow is
   $\Phi_t(q,p)=\bigl(q\cos t+p\sin t,\ -q\sin t+p\cos t\bigr)$, defined for all $t\in\mathbb R$;
2. the derivative $Y(t)=D\Phi_t(q,p)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&\sin t\\-\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}$
   satisfies $Y'(t)=J\,\mathrm{Hess}\,H\,Y(t)$, $Y(0)=I_2$,
   $Y(t)^{\mathsf T}J\,Y(t)=J$ and $\det Y(t)=1$ for all $t$, in accordance with
   [[prop-cm-flow-derivative-satisfies-the-canonical-matrix-identity]].
